summary: You must self-assess your fitness before every flight, whether you hold a Part-MED medical or a Pilot Medical Declaration. Stress, fatigue, dehydration, alcohol, medication and illness all reduce performance. The UK alcohol limit for flying is 20 mg per 100 ml, and the I AM SAFE checklist covers Illness, Attitude, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Eating. Hypoxia is a risk above 8,000 ft and carbon monoxide mimics it. Built from CAA Safety Sense Leaflet 24.
src: Safety Sense Leaflet 24: Pilot Health and Performance
sections: Factors that reduce performance
Stress: some is useful, too much hurts performance
Fatigue slows reactions and weakens concentration, memory and vigilance
Dehydration causes fatigue and headaches, worsened by hot cabins. Skipping meals gives low energy and mood swings
Alcohol: UK flying limit is 20 mg per 100 ml blood, stricter than driving. Alcohol in the last 24 hours can still give a positive result
Persistent low mood or anxiety harms concentration and decisions: pause and seek advice
I AM SAFE
Illness, Attitude, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating
Plan at least 8 hours sleep before flying
No flying within 8 hours of drinking, and up to 24 hours after a lot
Eat a moderate, healthy meal within a few hours of flight
Use it like a weather or NOTAM check before going to the aircraft
Medical certificates and the PMD
Private pilots need a UK Part-MED certificate or, where permitted, a Pilot Medical Declaration (PMD)
PMD standard: reasonable belief you meet DVLA Group 1 (car) standards. No examination, introduced 2016, with more restricted privileges (normally UK aircraft and airspace)
PMD maximum take-off mass limits: 2,000 kg or 5,700 kg depending on the requirements met
Class 2 covers PPL flying and is done by an AME. A LAPL medical can usually be done by a GP
Both systems rely on honesty. Seek aeromedical advice after surgery, regular medication, serious illness or injury, pregnancy, hospital admission, or needing glasses for the first time
Withdraw a PMD as soon as you stop meeting DVLA Group 1 standards
Medication, illness and incapacitation
Starting a new medicine: leave a few days before flying to see effects
SERA.2020 bars flying under a psychoactive substance that impairs performance. Be careful with strong pain relief such as codeine, tramadol or morphine
Heart, blood vessel and brain conditions are the most critical causes of sudden incapacitation
Severe pain, vertigo, sudden vision loss and severe gastroenteritis can incapacitate
Minor colds and earache can become serious in flight
Vision and hearing
Eye checks at least every two years. Cataracts often affect night vision first
Carry a spare pair of glasses or lenses. The CAA advises against polarised and photochromic lenses
Hearing loss, especially of high frequencies, makes radio speech harder. A good aviation headset helps
Altitude and gas effects
Trapped gas expands as you climb: ear, sinus and gut discomfort. Do not fly with a cold, and use the Valsalva technique to clear ears
Above 8,000 ft contrast sensitivity falls, especially in low light
Above 10,000 ft: confusion, clumsiness, drowsiness, alcohol-like effects
Without oxygen or pressurisation stay below 10,000 ft, and above that use supplementary oxygen per NCO.OP.190
If hypoxia is suspected, descend. Hyperventilation can be a sign of hypoxia or stress
Heat, cold, CO and G
Cockpits trap heat, especially while taxiing: drink water and wear breathable clothing
Cold reduces dexterity and slows reactions
Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless from exhaust and cabin heaters, and its symptoms resemble hypoxia
G-forces change blood flow to eyes and brain: aerobatic training covers the anti-G straining manoeuvre
Spatial disorientation and motion sickness
Balance sense can conflict with the aircraft's real attitude, leading to wrong control inputs
Risk is highest at night, in cloud, or with false horizons such as sloping cloud banks
If you enter cloud: trust the instruments, level the wings, stabilise, then look for visual references. Non-instrument pilots must never enter cloud deliberately
Motion sickness is a mismatch between vision and balance. If it starts, be ready to return early
Staying healthy
UK adult guidance: 150 minutes moderate or 75 minutes vigorous activity a week
Alcohol: not more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days
NHS Health Check every five years for ages 40 to 74 in England
Smoking and e-cigarettes raise heart disease risk

quiz.q: Which describes the alcohol rule for pilots?
o: No alcohol limit if not flying solo
quiz.why: The flying limit is 20 mg per 100 ml, much stricter than driving.

quiz.q: In I AM SAFE, what does the second A stand for?
quiz.why: Illness, Attitude, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating.

quiz.q: You start a new medication. What does the leaflet suggest?
o: Leave a few days before flying to see how it affects you
Fly immediately, as long as you feel well on the day
Fly only solo until you know how it affects you
Take a double dose the day before to test the effects
quiz.why: Side effects may be delayed, so wait and take aeromedical advice.

quiz.q: A Pilot Medical Declaration is based on meeting:
quiz.why: A PMD requires reasonable belief you meet DVLA Group 1 car standards.

quiz.q: Without oxygen or pressurisation, which ceiling applies?
quiz.why: Flights without oxygen or pressurisation must stay below 10,000 ft.

quiz.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning is hard to spot because:
o: It is colourless, odourless and mimics hypoxia
It has a strong smell that is easily confused
It only happens in winter with the heater on
It affects only passengers in the rear seats
quiz.why: CO is invisible and its symptoms resemble hypoxia.

quiz.q: Who is responsible for fitness to fly before each flight?
o: The pilot, whichever medical system applies
The AME who issued the medical certificate
The instructor who authorises the flight
The aircraft operator or flying club
quiz.why: Self-assessment before every flight is the pilot's responsibility.
